q: How does an auditor verify activity data in a GHG inventory?
title: How auditors verify activity data
short: An auditor checks activity data in three ways. They trace a sample of reported quantities back to invoices, bills and meter readings. They trace a sample of source documents forward into the totals to test completeness. And they reconcile your totals against independent records such as purchase ledgers, stock registers and production.
audience: Auditors, sustainability leads preparing for assurance

sections.h: Step 1: understand how the numbers were built
p: Before testing anything, the verifier maps the data flow: which documents feed each emission source, who enters them, which spreadsheet or system adds them up, and where factors are applied. ISO 14064-3 calls this assessing the risk of misstatement. Sources that are large, manual or estimated get the most testing.

sections.h: Step 2: vouching and tracing a sample
ul: Vouching (testing accuracy): pick reported lines, for example March diesel of 4,200 litres, and find the fuel invoice or slip that supports the quantity, unit, date and site.
Tracing (testing completeness): pick source documents from the purchase ledger or the discom account, and check each one appears in the inventory in the right month.
Sample size grows with the size of the source and the level of assurance. Large sources may be tested in full.

sections.h: Step 3: reconcile to records the carbon team does not control
ul: Fuel bought per invoices against accounts payable or the general ledger.
Fuel used against purchases adjusted for opening and closing stock in the store register.
Electricity units against the discom bills for every connection, including small ones.
Energy use against production: a month where output rose but kWh fell gets a question.

sections.h: Step 4: check periods, units and recalculation
p: Verifiers look for bills that straddle two reporting periods, kVAh read as kWh, kilolitres read as litres, and net-metered units counted as consumption. Then they recalculate a sample: quantity times the stated factor, to the stated rounding. Any difference above their materiality threshold is reported to you as a misstatement to correct.

example.title: Worked example: reconciling a year of diesel
lines: Opening stock 3,000 litres, closing stock 5,000 litres
Scope 1: 50,000 x 2.68 kg CO2 per litre (IPCC 2006 default) = 134,000 kg CO2, 134 t
If the inventory reports 52,000 litres instead, it overstates by 2,000 x 2.68 = 5,360 kg CO2
example.note: The stock register is the independent record here; without it, purchases are only a proxy for use.

senseible: Senseible links every line to its source invoice or bill, records a SHA-256 fingerprint of each file and keeps a hash-chained ledger, so a verifier can vouch and recalculate without hunting for paper. Its Verified status means its own rule checks passed; the sampling, reconciliation and opinion remain the auditor's work.
